title: Crossing the Divide: Israeli and Palestinian Entrepreneurs Bet on Business to Build Peace
summary: When Salah Hussein was 11, Israeli soldiers raided his family home in Nablus, leaving him traumatized. For years, any uniform triggered fear. Today, at 33, he's voluntarily tied his future to an Israeli Jew. Hussein is one of about 35 entrepreneurs in 50:50 Startups, an accelerator where mixed teams of Palestinians, Israeli Arabs, and Israeli Jews spend six months in a business bootcamp, culminating in a pitch session in Boston. His venture, Qanara Tech, uses AI-powered cameras to detect and prevent pests in greenhouses. His co-founder, Yana Shaulov, a 37-year-old molecular biologist from Haifa, joined hoping to launch her own idea but ended up on Hussein's team. "It's not always easy, you can feel the tension sometimes, but [Israelis and Palestinians] are both here to stay, and we have to live together at the end of the day," she says. The program, founded seven years ago by Amir Grinsteen, rests on the belief that building businesses together builds lasting bridges. Yet the collaboration adds an extra layer of difficulty to an already daunting endeavor—roughly 90% of startups fail. Beyond pragmatic needs like resources and capital, Hussein is driven by a refusal to pass on hatred to his children. "If we are not the ones looking for change, who will be?" he asks. The backlash can be intense. Hussein recalls a previous venture that collapsed after Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack and the ensuing war. Hardliners back home call him a "normalizer," and the scorn can seep into his own thoughts. But he counters the negativity: "Keep going, keep moving! All these tiny effects can lead to change." Israeli participants feel the strain too. Aviv Meir, 27, describes the mental challenge: "It's hard to put yourself in the enemy's shoes. You need to have so much strength to feel safe, and to understand that understanding their side will not demolish your side." The human friction was on display at a recent public event in Boston. Sarah Blum, a French Israeli, told Palestinian participant Salah Elsadi about a knife attack she survived a decade ago by a Palestinian man. Elsadi, who lived in Gaza for 15 years, was visibly shaken but listened as Blum emphasized the importance of dialogue. The moment underscored the program's raw, unresolved tensions—and its stubborn hope.
why_it_matters: This story shows how ordinary people use business to chip away at a conflict that often seems frozen, but it also reveals the huge psychological cost and social blowback. For youth inheriting these conflicts, it raises the question of whether economic cooperation can succeed where politics has repeatedly failed.

background_read: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict has lasted for decades, with cycles of violence and failed peace talks leaving deep mistrust on both sides. Nablus, where Salah Hussein grew up, is a Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank that has seen frequent military raids and clashes.

The militant group Hamas, which governs the Gaza Strip, carried out an unprecedented attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, killing about 1,200 people and triggering a devastating war that worsened tensions between Israelis and Palestinians worldwide.

People-to-people peace efforts have tried business and cultural exchanges before. For example, after the 1990s Oslo Accords, joint Israeli–Palestinian industrial zones were proposed, though most faded as violence returned. 50:50 Startups follows a similar logic—believing that shared economic stakes can slowly rebuild trust, even when political solutions seem far away.
The Boston pitch event connects Middle Eastern founders with American investors, echoing a long tradition of using a neutral third country to host difficult dialogues.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue that joint businesses create practical reasons to cooperate and can gradually erode stereotypes. When Israelis and Palestinians succeed together, they model a different future, showing that coexistence is possible even when governments are at odds. The programme, though tiny, offers a concrete alternative to endless cycles of violence.

Critics note that hardliners on both sides see such collaborations as ‘normalization’ that betrays their cause, which can lead to social ostracism and danger. Moreover, the collapse of a previous venture after the October 7 attack shows how fragile these links are—a single violent event can undo years of trust-building. Some argue that business alone cannot address the underlying injustice or occupation.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral – historical pattern of economic peace attempts
perspectives.description: Throughout history, economic projects have been tried in conflict zones, from Northern Ireland to the Balkans, with mixed results. Often they work best when a political peace process is underway, and become strained when violence escalates. The 50:50 Startups model fits this pattern: it builds pockets of cooperation that may survive but rarely transform the wider conflict on their own.

If the programme can expand beyond 35 entrepreneurs and attract long-term investment, it might create a critical mass of business ties that make a return to violence more costly for those communities. However, for real change, such efforts would need to be paired with political dialogue and a reduction of the occupation. The next test is whether the human bonds forged now can withstand another round of war.
